entry.definition: Showing skills or maturity much earlier than usual, especially as a child.
entry.example: Her precocious questions about the stars led her parents to buy her a telescope when she was five.
entry.nuance: Precocious stresses that abilities appear unusually early, while gifted describes talent at any age; precocious can also hint at a child acting cheekily grown-up.
entry.prompt: A teacher describes one of the students in her second-grade class.
options: The precocious seven-year-old was already solving fifth-grade fractions.
The precocious pile of books on her desk looked ready to tumble onto the floor.
The precocious student was the last in her class to learn to tie her shoes.
The precocious gold sticker was so dear to her that she kept it in a locked box.
reasons: A young child doing math meant for older students is developing ahead of schedule.
This confuses the word with precarious; an unstable pile has nothing to do with early development.
Lagging behind classmates is the reverse of reaching milestones early.
This mixes the word up with precious; a treasured object cannot mature early.

practice.prompt: A music instructor talks about the campers at a summer piano program.
options: The precocious teenager had only just learned to find middle C on the keyboard.
At nine, the precocious pianist was writing short sonatas of her own.
The precocious bench wobbled every time a camper leaned toward the keys.
The precocious toddler could clap along to a song, just as most toddlers can.
reasons: Learning a basic skill late points to slow progress, not early mastery.
Composing original music at such a young age is far ahead of what most children can do.
A shaky seat is precarious, not advanced for its age.
Doing what is ordinary for one's age is not unusually early at all.
